inline.s: [Trichiliocosm] That is, a great trichiliocosm; it is the region taught and transformed by one Buddha. One Mount Sumeru together with the four great continents is called a small world. A thousand small worlds gathered together is called a “small trichiliocosm”; a thousand small trichiliocosms gathered together is called a “middle trichiliocosm”; a thousand middle trichiliocosms gathered together is called a “great trichiliocosm.” Because “thousand” is used three times, a great trichiliocosm is also called a “trichiliocosm.” [Mount Sumeru] Rendered into Chinese as Wonderful High Mountain, it is the center of a small world. This mountain is made of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli and crystal—and no other mountain can compare with its height; it is the king of mountains. [The four great continents] Around Mount Sumeru there are four great continents: the eastern one is called Purvavideha, the southern one is called Jambudvipa (the world we live in is in this continent), the western one is called Aparagodaniya, and the northern one is called Uttarakuru. [Seven treasures] Gold, silver, lapis lazuli, glass (similar to crystal; more than two thousand years ago there was no such thing as what we now call glass), tridacna shell, red pearl and agate. [Would they be many?] Would they not be many indeed? [Would] Could it be that.
Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One! Why is this? This merit and virtue is not the nature of merit and virtue, and so the Tathagata says the merit and virtue is great”

—Subhuti replied: Very great, World-Honored One! Why is this? This merit and virtue is not a truly existing entity, but an illusion, a matter within the dream of ignorance; and it is precisely because merit and virtue is an illusion that there can be talk of more or less. (This is because “more” and “less” are concepts within the dream of ignorance.) Therefore the Tathagata says this merit and virtue is great.

[Is not the nature of merit and virtue] The Notes on the Doctrine of Consciousness-Only say: “Nature means essence.” Merit and virtue is a matter within the dream of ignorance, having marks but no essence. “Is not the nature of merit and virtue” means that merit and virtue is not truly existent, but is an illusion.

[If again there is a person who receives and upholds even four lines of verse from this sutra and explains it for others, that person’s merit surpasses the other’s. Why is this? Subhuti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra. Subhuti, what are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma.]

Note: In this passage of the sutra, the last sentence of the current circulated edition reads: “Subhuti! What are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma.” In the Qianlong Tripitaka there are no such four characters as “therefore they are called Buddha and dharma.” However, the Chen
dynasty translation by the Tripitaka Master Paramartha reads: “Subhuti! What is spoken of as Buddha and dharma is not Buddha and dharma; therefore it is called Buddha and dharma.” The Tang

dynasty translation by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang reads: “Subhuti! As to Buddhas and dharmas—Buddhas and dharmas—the Tathagata speaks of them as not Buddhas and dharmas; therefore the Tathagata speaks of them as Buddhas and dharmas, Buddhas and dharmas.” The Tang
dynasty translation by Yijing reads: “Therefore, Subhuti! As to Buddha and dharma, the Tathagata speaks of them as not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma.”
If again there is a person who receives and upholds this sutra, or even four lines of verse, and explains it for others, that person’s merit surpasses the other’s”

—The World-Honored One said: If there is another person who receives and upholds the whole of this sutra, or a part of it, or even only a single verse (four lines of text), and expounds it for others, the merit and virtue so obtained surpasses the merit and virtue obtained by the person before who gave in charity seven treasures filling a trichiliocosm.
This sentence breaks the mark of non-dharma.

[Verse] A short form of “gatha,” it is a rhymed composition somewhat like poetry, usually taking four lines as one verse. A verse is the basic unit of a sutra, and the size of a sutra is usually expressed by how many verses it contains; for example, the

Zhenyuan Record of Buddhist Teachings, fascicle seventeen, says: “The Sanskrit text of the Mahavaipulya Buddha Avatamsaka Sutra has six bundles in all, one hundred thousand verses altogether.” Here “four lines of verse” refers generally to any four lines in the sutra. Someone asked Master Hanshan: The four lines of the Diamond Sutra—what exactly are they? The great masters of old each gave a different answer, and there was no settled wording. Why? The Master replied: “The prajna taught by the Buddha is like the myriad grasses on the Snow Mountain—every one of them is medicine; picked up and used, each will certainly cure the illness. So when the ancients pointed out what the four lines are, each merely picked one stalk of grass from the Snow Mountain.” (Dream Roam Collection,

“Eight Items of Instruction Requested by Lord Kaigong of Jizhao”) [The myriad grasses of the Snow Mountain] On the Snow Mountain there are numinous herbs; whoever sees them gains immeasurable lifespan. The Nirvana Sutra says: “Within the Snow Mountain there is a supreme fragrant medicine named Saha; whoever sees it gains immeasurable lifespan and is free of sickness and suffering.”

[Receiving and upholding] “Receiving” is to accept: through understanding the principle and the path of the dharma in the sutra, one gives rise to faith, and so one sincerely accepts it. “Upholding” is to put it into practice, carrying out the principle and the path of the dharma in the sutra. As it is said: understand the sutra and attain the dharma; practice according to the dharma. [Receiving and upholding even four lines of verse, and explaining them for others] Either receiving and upholding all of it, or a part of it, or even only a single verse (four lines), and explaining it for others.
Why is this? Subhuti, all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra”

—Why is it that receiving and upholding the Diamond Sutra, or even four lines of verse, and explaining them for others, yields merit and virtue as great as this? Subhuti, it is because this sutra is the mind-dharma of all Buddhas: all Buddhas attain the Way by reliance on this sutra, and the dharma by which all Buddhas become Buddhas comes forth from this sutra.
Question: Why is it said that “all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra”?
Answer: On this question, the layman Jiang Weinong, in his
Commentary on the Diamond Sutra
, gives a most incisive exposition:
“In reading the sutra and hearing the dharma, what matters is to be deeply watchful and apprehensive
(fearful of transgression)
and to take what the Buddha has said as a mirror, at all times and in all places using it to reflect oneself
(to examine whether one’s body, speech and mind accord with what the Buddha said—accord, and one is awakened; fail to accord, and one is deluded)

. If one does not observe and does not reflect, how can delusion become awakening? This is what is meant by relying on the words to give rise to contemplation. When the work of contemplation has long endured, then a sense of solemn watchfulness arises of itself; this is initial awakening. It is also the first opening of the right wisdom inherent in the principle-essence. Thus, without retreat and without slackening, the work of contemplation grows deeper and purer day by day. Then what is called initial awakening is first like the new moon, gradually more light and less
(same as “dark”)

darkness; until the moon’s disc is full and its radiance shines forth, and then the essence of the nature manifests. This is initial awakening merging with original awakening, and there is then no division between initial and original. You should know that to become a Buddha is nothing other than the perfect clarity of the awakened nature. And the opening of the awakened nature cannot come about except by relying on the power of the prajna of words. Therefore it is said: all Buddhas come forth from this sutra.”
Subhuti, what are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma”
—Subhuti! What are called Buddha and dharma (having marks) are not Buddha and dharma (without essence); therefore they are called Buddha and dharma (they are illusions).
This sentence breaks the mark of dharma. The view of Buddha and the view of dharma are done away with—how much less could the affliction-view of living beings arise?

[Buddha and dharma] The “Buddha” in this sentence refers to “all Buddhas” in the preceding sentence, “all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra”; “dharma” refers to “the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas” in this sentence.

As for Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment being illusions, in the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment the Buddha says: “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in space.” He also says: “Birth and death and nirvana, ordinary beings and all Buddhas, are alike the marks of empty flowers.” The Lankavatara Sutra says: “There is no Buddha of nirvana, no nirvana of Buddha.” In the
Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra, Chapter Three on Habitual Conformity, the Buddha says: “There is no Buddha, and no Buddha Way.” The Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra,

Chapter Eleven on the Illusory, says: “The four foundations of mindfulness are not different from illusion, illusion is not different from the four foundations of mindfulness; the four foundations of mindfulness are illusion, illusion is the four foundations of mindfulness; and so on up to supreme, perfect enlightenment, which is not different from illusion, illusion is not different from supreme, perfect enlightenment; supreme, perfect enlightenment is illusion, illusion is supreme, perfect enlightenment.” In the seventeenth section of this sutra, the Buddha says: “Subhuti! In truth there is no dharma by which the Tathagata attains supreme, perfect enlightenment. Subhuti! If there were a dharma by which the Tathagata attained supreme, perfect enlightenment, then Burning Lamp Buddha would not have given me the prediction: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni.’ Because in truth there is no dharma by which one attains supreme, perfect enlightenment, therefore Burning Lamp Buddha gave me the prediction, saying: ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni.’”

This section says that the merit and virtue of receiving and upholding this sutra is inconceivable, because this one scroll of the Diamond Sutra is the mind-dharma of all Buddhas: all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra.

Before this, the World-Honored One had all along been breaking living beings’ deluded view of clinging to the teachings of the sutras; but he also feared that living beings might go to the other extreme—denying and belittling the teachings and the dharma of the sutras, and falling into the dark abyss of ignorance. So here he says: the merit and virtue of upholding the sutra is inconceivable, and all Buddhas and the dharmas of supreme, perfect enlightenment of all Buddhas all come forth from this sutra. Yet, fearing again that living beings might falsely cling to this as real, he once more admonishes: “What are called Buddha and dharma are not Buddha and dharma; therefore they are called Buddha and dharma.” Truly this is painstaking solicitude: again and again, over and over, he patiently guides us living beings, teaching that we must neither cling to marks nor annihilate marks, but must be skilled at using the false to cultivate the true, using illusion to leave illusion, until illusions are exhausted and the dream awakens.

Question: The Diamond Sutra says: “All forms whatsoever are false and unreal.” The Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment also says: “All Buddha-worlds are like flowers in space.” Since the Buddha-worlds are illusory, why should one still seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land?

Answer: If in this present life we could leave all marks entirely and become Buddhas, waking from the dream, that would of course be best. But we cannot do it: even a bodhisattva of the first stage of faith must pass through fifty-two stages and three great asamkhyeya kalpas before becoming a Buddha and waking from the dream of ignorance. Though each stage is still illusion, each is closer than the last to the goal of waking from the dream—this is using illusion to leave illusion, until illusions are exhausted and the dream awakens. The three realms are like a burning house; illusory though they are, our knowing mind is not yet exhausted and we are still within the dream, feeling the keen pain of birth, aging, sickness and death—truly a suffering beyond words, scorched and tormented! And once this human body is lost, it is hard to regain it even in ten thousand kalpas, and who knows in what age one will hear the Buddha-dharma again! Therefore the first step is that in this very life one must certainly escape these three realms of birth-and-death and rebirth.

We are now in the age of the decline of the dharma; seeking rebirth in the Western Pure Land through Buddha-recitation is the one truly practicable road. The Great Collection Sutra says: “In the age of the dharma’s decline, among hundreds of millions of people who cultivate, scarcely one attains the Way; only by relying on Buddha-recitation can one cross over birth and death.” Mazu founded the monastic groves (Chan monasteries), and Baizhang established the pure rules. Great Master Baizhang Dazhi’s “Essential Rules of the Monastic Grove” (at that time it was not yet the age of decline, and so many who cultivated Chan attained realization) begins by saying: “A monastic grove prospers through having no affairs; in cultivation, Buddha-recitation is the safe course.” For the ordinary path to ending birth and death requires cutting off the afflictions of view and thought, whereas rebirth in the Western Pure Land requires only that the afflictions be suppressed—compared with the other, this is far easier. Therefore in cultivation, Buddha-recitation is the safe course.

Furthermore, even if the afflictions of view and thought are exhausted and one can by one’s own power end fragmentary birth-and-death, still, having left the three realms, there remains an extremely long road to travel in ending transformational birth-and-death. Having reached the Western Pure Land, one has not only ended fragmentary birth-and-death but also possesses the best conditions for study and practice with which to end transformational birth-and-death: Amitabha Buddha, Avalokiteshvara Bodhisattva and Mahasthamaprapta Bodhisattva are one’s teachers, the great bodhisattvas are one’s fellow practitioners and friends, and one may go to the Buddha-realms of the ten directions to study. Moreover, the Buddha Speaks of Amitabha Sutra says: “In the Land of Ultimate Bliss, all who are born there are avaivartika.” Avaivartika means non-retrogression: they are not disturbed by any demons, and never fall back from the path to Buddhahood. This is the name of a bodhisattva stage, reached only after cultivation through one great asamkhyeya kalpa; yet we need only be reborn in the Pure Land to reach this stage and never fall back again. Therefore in the Chapter on the Vows and Practices of Samantabhadra in the Avatamsaka Sutra, Samantabhadra Bodhisattva’s ten kingly vows (the most supreme of vows being called kingly vows) guide all back to the Pure Land: “From empty space the sea of waking springs; through Saha’s realm the contrary current sings. For one who seeks the farther shore to gain, the Pure Land holds a boat to bear him home again.” Amitabha Buddha is also named Buddha of Infinite Light, and the Buddha-land of Infinite Light is the Western Pure Land. Here we should carefully realize and embody the World-Honored One’s teaching in the sixth section: “One should not grasp at non-dharma.” By no means should one fail to board the jeweled ship and instead try to swim the sea alone. Therefore Chan Master Zhongfeng says: “The ocean of enlightenment rises from empty space, the Saha world flows with contrary waves; if a person would reach the other shore, the Pure Land has a returning boat.” Once we reach the Pure Land, there is a great dharma-ship of treasure that will carry us smoothly and swiftly to the other shore of nirvana, and then we return into the sea of suffering among the dusty realms to save all living beings throughout the dharma-realm.
On this question, Chan Master Chewu, the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school, gives a most incisive teaching (see the

Collected Writings of Chan Master Chewu, first fascicle): “A Chan practitioner asked: All dharmas are wholly like a dream. The Saha world is certainly a dream, and the Pure Land is also a dream. Since both are one and the same dream, what benefit is there in cultivating it? I (Chan Master Chewu) replied: Not so! Before the seventh stage, one cultivates the Way within a dream. As for the great dream of ignorance, even a bodhisattva of equal enlightenment still sleeps. Only the Buddha alone is called one who is greatly awakened. While the eye of the dream is not yet opened, suffering and joy are vividly present. Rather than suffer the extreme suffering of the Saha world in a dream, why not enjoy the wonderful bliss of the Pure Land in a dream? Moreover, the dream of the Saha world goes from dream into dream, dreaming and dreaming again, tossing and sinking ever deeper. The dream of the Pure Land goes from dream into awakening, awakening and awakening again, gradually arriving at great awakening. The dreams are alike, but that by which one dreams is by no means alike! Can they be lumped together?”

[Chan Master Chewu] A man of the Qianlong and Jiaqing reigns of the Qing dynasty, his religious name was Jixing and his style Chewu. He awakened greatly through Chan practice and was the thirty-sixth patriarch of the Linji school. He once admired the life of Chan Master Yongming Yanshou, and so settled his mind on the Pure Land and espoused the Lotus school. Each day he limited his meetings with visitors to one stick of incense; beyond that he only bowed and recited. Whenever the Master expounded the dharma, it poured forth like a bottle upturned or clouds rising, with unhindered eloquence, and the winds of the Lotus school blew mightily; he became the twelfth patriarch of the Pure Land school. The Master knew in advance the time of his passing: on the seventeenth day of the twelfth month of the fifteenth year of Jiaqing, facing west with palms joined, he sat upright reciting the Buddha’s name and, seeing the Buddha reach down to guide him, passed away; the assembly smelled a rare fragrance floating in the air. He was enshrined for seven days, his countenance as if alive, kindly and full, his white hair turned black and its luster extraordinary.

[Seventh stage] From ordinary being to Buddhahood, a bodhisattva must pass through fifty-two stages in all: ten stages of faith, ten stages of dwelling, ten stages of practice, ten stages of dedication, ten stages of grounding, equal enlightenment, and wonderful enlightenment (when the stage of wonderful enlightenment is complete, one becomes a Buddha). The seventh of the ten groundings is called the “seventh stage.” [Equal enlightenment] Of the fifty-two stages, the fifty-first is called equal enlightenment: the bodhisattva who has completed the ten groundings and is about to realize the fruit of Buddhahood, whose merit and wisdom are nearly equal to the Buddha’s; hence the name “equal enlightenment.”

Question: We recite the Buddha’s name and seek rebirth in the Western Pure Land, and a great virtuous one has said, “As to being born, one is certainly born; as to going, one in truth does not go.” How should this be understood?

Answer: The saying “As to being born, one is certainly born; as to going, one in truth does not go” comes from Great Master Yihuai of the Song dynasty. The Master was a dharma-heir of Chongxian, the reviver of the Yunmen school; he dedicated his whole life to the Pure Land and wrote the Treatise Resolving Doubts About the Pure Land. “As to being born, one is certainly born” means: rebirth is the consciousness going to the Western Pure Land and no longer undergoing birth and death and rebirth—this truly happens and is not fiction. “As to going, one in truth does not go” means: rebirth in the Western Pure Land is likewise a matter within the dream of ignorance, its essence not truly existing; hence it is said that “in truth one does not go.” This is also the principle taught in the next section, “One Mark and No Mark, Section Nine,” for example: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can a srotapanna think, ‘I have attained the fruit of srotapanna’? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A srotapanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet in truth he has not entered anything, and does not enter forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; therefore he is called a srotapanna.” The Commentary on the Diamond Sutra says: “You should know that when Amitabha comes to receive them, he has never actually come; and being reborn in the West, they have never actually gone. Yet though they have never gone, what harm is there in appearing to come and to go? Why is this? The one who neither comes nor goes is the principle-essence; there is coming and going in the marks of things. Principle and phenomena have never been two, and nature and marks must be perfectly interfused. Therefore, although there is neither coming nor going, that does not hinder there being coming and going; and although there is coming and going, in truth there is neither coming nor going. What matters most is this: coming and going must be recognized in the neither-coming-nor-going, and the neither-coming-nor-going must be put into practice in the coming and going. This is the essential secret of reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth. Having obtained this essential secret, one will certainly be reborn and see the Buddha. Who says that cultivating the Pure Land requires no study of prajna, and even suspects that prajna obstructs the Pure Land?”

This section says: even one who has realized the fruit should not think, “I have attained the fruit”; one should leave marks in this way. Here the World-Honored One takes the four fruits that Subhuti himself realized (the fruit of srotapanna, the fruit of sakridagamin, the fruit of anagamin and the fruit of arhat) as examples for breaking the mark of dharma, which makes it all the more intimate.

[One mark, no mark] This means that the various marks are all illusions (“all forms whatsoever are false and unreal”), and their substance is a single mark (one mark)—nothing whatsoever; this is no mark. Just as one who dreams sees the things in the dream as manifold and varied, with all kinds of marks, yet for one whose eyes are open there is nothing at all, and this sole mark of there being nothing at all is no mark. The Buddha says: “The marks of all dharmas are all one mark, which is called no mark.” (Buddha Treasury Sutra,
Chapter One on the True Nature of All Dharmas)

What precedes speaks of non-dwelling—not dwelling in marks, because “all forms whatsoever are false and unreal.” This section speaks of the cultivation of no mark—the unconditioned dharma—which is a further step in the practice. Above, the World-Honored One said that the fruit of Buddhahood, which he himself realized, is unattainable; here the section says: Subhuti, the fruit that you have realized is likewise unattainable—“no srotapanna, no fruit of srotapanna; no sakridagamin, no fruit of sakridagamin; no anagamin, no fruit of anagamin; no arhat, no fruit of arhat.”
In the
Mahaprajnaparamita Sutra

, Chapter Three on Habitual Conformity, the Buddha says: “Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, accumulation, extinction or path; no wisdom and no attainment; no srotapanna, no fruit of srotapanna, no sakridagamin, no fruit of sakridagamin, no anagamin, no fruit of anagamin, no arhat, no fruit of arhat, no pratyekabuddha, no path of pratyekabuddha; no Buddha, and no Buddha Way. Shariputra, when a bodhisattva-mahasattva thus cultivates conformity, this is called corresponding with the prajnaparamita.”
Here a few terms need explaining, to make the sutra text below easier to understand; readers already familiar with these terms and marks may simply skip this.

[Mahayana] That is, the bodhisattva’s approach, whose principle is to save the world and benefit others, and whose highest fruit is Buddhahood. From ordinary being to Buddhahood, the Mahayana has fifty-two stages, namely: ten stages of faith (“ten” indicates that ten stages are contained within, and the same applies below), ten stages of dwelling, ten stages of practice, ten stages of dedication, ten stages of grounding, equal enlightenment, and wonderful enlightenment (the fruit of Buddhahood). “Yana” means “vehicle”; it is a metaphor for the Buddha-dharma as a ferryboat that can carry living beings from this shore of birth and death across to the other shore of nirvana. The bodhisattva vehicle saves many living beings, and so is called the Great Vehicle; the shravaka vehicle and the pratyekabuddha vehicle save few living beings, and so are called the Small Vehicle. [Small Vehicle] The approach of the shravakas and pratyekabuddhas, whose principle is to cultivate oneself and benefit oneself. [Shravaka vehicle] Those who awaken to the Way by hearing the Buddha’s voice and cultivating the four noble truths. The shravaka vehicle has four fruits: the fruit of srotapanna (first fruit), the fruit of sakridagamin (second fruit), the fruit of anagamin (third fruit) and the fruit of arhat (fourth fruit). To realize the fruit of arhat is to escape birth and death and leave the three realms. [Pratyekabuddha vehicle] The pratyekabuddha vehicle is also called the middle vehicle; it cultivates the twelve links of dependent origination, and its highest fruit is the fruit of pratyekabuddha. From ordinary being up to pratyekabuddha, its cultivation emphasizes awakening and realization—wherever awakening reaches, realization reaches—and so there are no clear stages to speak of. [The four noble truths] Also called the four holy truths, namely the truth of suffering, the truth of accumulation, the truth of extinction and the truth of the path (abbreviated as suffering, accumulation, extinction and path); “truth” here means ultimate reality. The truth of suffering explains the reality that life is full of suffering; the “accumulation” of the truth of accumulation means “drawing together,” and it explains the reality of how life’s suffering comes about; the truth of extinction explains the reality that only the state of nirvana is the ultimate extinction of suffering; the truth of the path explains the reality of how one must cultivate the Way in order to realize nirvana. These four noble truths fully cover the two layers of cause and effect within and beyond the world: accumulation is the cause and suffering is the fruit—this is the cause and effect of the deluded realm; the path is the cause and extinction is the fruit—this is the cause and effect of the awakened realm. [The twelve links of dependent origination] They explain the process by which sentient beings flow through birth and death. The twelve links are: ignorance (afflictions such as greed, anger and delusion—this is the root of birth and death), formation (the doing of various karmas), consciousness (the karmic consciousness entering a womb), name-and-form (there being only an embryonic form, the six senses not yet complete), the six sense-bases (the fetus growing into a human form complete with the six senses of eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind), contact (emerging from the womb and coming into contact with outer conditions), feeling (contact with outer conditions giving rise to feelings of suffering and pleasure), craving (desire arising toward conditions), grasping (seeking and doing), becoming (forming karmic causes able to bring about future retribution), birth (receiving a future body of the five aggregates), and aging-and-death (that future body gradually aging and dying). These twelve links cover all the causes and effects of the three periods of time—giving rise to delusion, creating karma and receiving birth—revolving without end and continuing into infinity.

[The five aggregates] Form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness—the five great elements that constitute a human body. Of these, the aggregate of form (matter) is the body, and the remaining four aggregates (feeling, perception, formation and consciousness) are the mind. The five aggregates were formerly translated as the five shadows. The Nirvana Sutra says: “At the time of death, relatives weep. The person is terrified and cannot keep hold of himself. All the good and evil of a lifetime appears before him. After the last warmth is gone, the past five shadows cease and the present intermediate existence arises. After entering the womb, the present intermediate existence ceases and the future five shadows arise. It is like a lamp being lit as darkness is extinguished, and the lamp going out as darkness arises, continuing without interruption.” [Feeling] The mental function whereby the contact of sense-faculty with object gives rise to feelings of suffering, pleasure, or neither-suffering-nor-pleasure. [Perception] The mental function that, relying on feeling, gives rise to imagining about things, or to choices of acceptance and rejection, meeting and refusing. [Formation] The mental function that, relying on imagining and choosing, gives rise to good and evil actions. [Consciousness] The distinguishing and cognizing of the objects of the senses.

[Worldly and world-transcending] The worldly and the world-transcending. The worldly is the world of ordinary beings of the six paths (hells, hungry ghosts, animals, asuras, humans and gods); the world-transcending is the world of arhats, pratyekabuddhas, bodhisattvas and Buddhas. [The two kinds of delusion] Delusion of view and delusion of thought. Delusion of view is incorrect knowledge and seeing, such as the five wrong views—the view of a body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of clinging to ascetic practices and precepts. Delusion of thought, also called delusion of cultivation, consists of the delusions of greed, anger, delusion, pride and doubt. Cutting off these two delusions of view and thought, one realizes the fruit of arhat and leaves the three realms. Moreover, delusion of view is an intellectual affliction, cut off at the moment of seeing the Way, and so it is also called “what is cut off by seeing”; delusion of thought is a habitual affliction, innate and inborn, which can be cut off only through long cultivation, and so it is also called “what is cut off by cultivation.” [The five wrong views] Also called the five evil views, namely the view of a body, extreme views, wrong views, the view of grasping at views, and the view of clinging to ascetic practices and precepts. The “view of a body” is clinging to the body falsely compounded of the five aggregates as truly existing. “Extreme views” are evil views leaning to one side: for example, some people hold that after death everything returns to nothing, that a person dies as a lamp goes out—this is called the view of annihilation; others hold that after death one is still a human, and that pigs, horses, cattle and sheep after death are still pigs, horses, cattle and sheep—this is called the view of permanence. Both the view of annihilation and the view of permanence lean to one side, and so are called extreme views. “Wrong views” are views that are false and not right, such as denying cause and effect and destroying all good deeds. “The view of grasping at views” is to cling to the three wrong views above (the view of a body, extreme views and wrong views) as correct. “The view of clinging to ascetic practices and precepts” is to undertake false precepts and mistakenly take them as right precepts: for example, some people smear themselves with ash (the ash-smearing ascetics were one of the ancient Indian non-Buddhist schools, who covered their whole bodies with ash and sought rebirth in heaven through austerities) and fast, mistakenly believing this to be the way of liberation.

[Subhuti, what do you think? Can a srotapanna think, “I have attained the fruit of srotapanna”? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A srotapanna is called one who has entered the stream, yet he has not entered anything, and does not enter forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; therefore he is called a srotapanna.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can one who has attained the first fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of srotapanna”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because a srotapanna is called “one who has entered the stream” (entered the holy stream) precisely because he has entered nothing (he has left marks) and does not enter the six dusts (he can empty emotional consciousness and leave the marks of forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles and dharmas); therefore he is called a srotapanna. If he still clung to marks as to something entered (thinking that he had gained something in cultivation), then he would not be called a srotapanna.

[Srotapanna] Rendered into Chinese as “one who has entered the stream,” meaning one who has for the first time entered the stream of the sages, because he has already cut off the delusion of view completely; at most he will go back and forth between the human and heavenly realms for seven rebirths, and will certainly realize the fruit of arhat.

The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters Spoken by the Buddha says: “The arhat can fly and transform himself, has a lifespan of vast kalpas, and his abiding moves heaven and earth. Next is the anagamin. The anagamin, at the end of his life, sends his spirit (his consciousness) up to the nineteen heavens and realizes arhatship. Next is the sakridagamin. The sakridagamin, with one going up and one returning, then attains arhatship. Next is the srotapanna. The srotapanna, through seven deaths and seven births, then realizes arhatship.”

[Subhuti, what do you think? Can a sakridagamin think, “I have attained the fruit of sakridagamin”? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? A sakridagamin is called one who returns once, yet in truth there is no coming or going; therefore he is called a sakridagamin.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can one who has attained the second fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of sakridagamin”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because although a sakridagamin must go once up to the heavens and come once back to the human realm in order to cut off the delusion of thought and realize the fruit of arhat, all of this is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and so in truth there is no coming or going; therefore he is called a sakridagamin.

[Sakridagamin] Rendered into Chinese: “one who returns once.” The delusion of thought (greed, anger, delusion, pride and doubt) is the subtlest, an innate and inborn affliction, divided into ten grades. After a cultivator has cut off the delusion of view completely and realized the first fruit, he then cuts off the first six grades of the delusion of thought and realizes the second fruit (sakridagamin). After that he must still go once up to the heavens and come once back to the human realm, continuing to cut off the delusion of thought in order to realize the third fruit (anagamin), and then in the four dhyana heavens of the form realm cut off the delusion of thought completely and realize the fourth fruit (arhat). Taken as a whole, it is one going up to the heavens and one returning to the human realm before realizing the fruit of arhat; hence the name “one who returns once.”

[Subhuti, what do you think? Can an anagamin think, “I have attained the fruit of anagamin”? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? An anagamin is called one who does not come, yet in truth there is no not-coming; therefore he is called an anagamin.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can one who has attained the third fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of anagamin”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because although an anagamin is called “one who does not come” (does not come to the human realm to receive birth), all of this is a matter within the dream of ignorance, and so in truth there is no not-coming; therefore he is called an anagamin.

[Anagamin] Rendered into Chinese: “one who does not return.” After a cultivator has realized the second fruit, he then cuts off three more grades of the delusion of thought and realizes the third fruit. One who reaches this fruit dwells in the four dhyana heavens of the form realm and there realizes the fruit of arhat, and no longer comes to the human realm to receive birth; hence the name “one who does not return.”

[Subhuti, what do you think? Can an arhat think, “I have attained the way of arhat”? Subhuti said: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? In truth there is no dharma named arhat. World-Honored One, if an arhat were to think, “I have attained the way of arhat,” he would then be clinging to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think? Can one who has attained the fourth fruit think, “I have attained the fruit of arhat”? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One. Why is this? Because the dharma “named arhat” (its phenomenal aspect) is not truly existent. If an arhat still had the thought “I have attained the fruit of arhat,” he would be falsely clinging to all dharmas as truly existing (clinging to self, person, sentient beings and lifespan), and he would not be an arhat.

[Arhat] Rendered into Chinese: “one without birth.” After a cultivator has realized the third fruit, he cuts off the last grade of the delusion of thought in the four dhyana heavens; his afflictions are exhausted and he receives no further existence (since the arhat’s afflictions and karma of birth and death are exhausted, he no longer receives a body in a later life, and so it is said that he “receives no further existence”). Birth and death are ended from then on, and so he is called “one without birth”; this is the highest fruit of the shravaka vehicle. [Attaining the way of arhat] Attaining the fruit of arhat. The Chen

dynasty translation by Paramartha reads: “Subhuti! What do you think? Can an arhat think: I have attained the fruit of arhat?” [In truth there is no dharma named arhat] This sentence means: there really is no such thing as “there being a dharma named arhat.” That is to say, “there being a dharma named arhat” is a matter within the dream of ignorance and is not truly existent. Subhuti says: the realization of the fruit of arhat is an illusion and not truly existent, and at the same time he does not have the thought that he has attained arhat (he does not cling to the mark of arhat). This is the cultivation of no mark, what is called “cultivating yet not cultivating.” “Cultivating” means applying effort; “not cultivating” means not clinging to the mark of cultivation. Cultivation is turning delusion into awakening, and clinging to marks is itself delusion; therefore cultivation that clings to marks cannot succeed—as it is said, boiling sand cannot make rice. The cultivation of no mark is the unconditioned dharma; cultivation that clings to marks is the conditioned dharma.

[World-Honored One, the Buddha says that I have attained the samadhi of non-contention, and am foremost among men, the foremost arhat free of desire. World-Honored One, I do not think, “I am an arhat free of desire.” World-Honored One, if I were to think, “I have attained the way of arhat,” the World-Honored One would not say that Subhuti delights in the practice of aranya. Because Subhuti in truth practices nothing, he is called one who delights in the practice of aranya.]

Subhuti continued: World-Honored One, the Buddha says that I have attained the samadhi of non-contention, that I am foremost among men, the foremost arhat free of desire. But I do not think in this way, that I am an arhat free of desire, and still less would I think that I am the foremost arhat free of desire. World-Honored One, if I thought in this way, that I had realized the fruit of arhat, the Buddha would not say that Subhuti is a cultivator who delights in the practice of non-contention. It is precisely because Subhuti does not act with clinging to marks, and has no discriminating mind of attainment or non-attainment, that the Buddha says Subhuti is a cultivator who delights in the practice of non-contention.

[Samadhi of non-contention] A meditative concentration without a discriminating mind, single-flavored and equal. [Free of desire] Without seeking and without clinging. The Sutra of Forty-Two Chapters says: “After the World-Honored One had attained the Way, he thought thus: freedom from desire and quiescence are the most supreme.” [Aranya] Rendered into Chinese as “non-contention,” also called “quiescence.” [Delighting in the practice of aranya] Delighting in the practice of non-contention. “Delighting” means loving it to the utmost, the mind and the practice according with one another.
Adorning the Buddha Land”—the Vimalakirti Sutra,

Chapter One on the Buddha-Land, says: “As his mind is pure, so are all his merits pure. Therefore, Ratnakara! If a bodhisattva wishes to attain a pure land, he should purify his mind; as his mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure.” This section enters the core and sets forth the mind-ground Dharma-gate—“all bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” As his mind is pure, so is the Buddha-land pure (adorning the Buddha Land); leaving marks must begin here.

[The Buddha told Subhuti: What do you think? When the Tathagata was formerly with Burning Lamp Buddha, did he obtain any dharma? No, World-Honored One. When the Tathagata was with Burning Lamp Buddha, he in truth obtained no dharma.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: What do you think—when the Tathagata was formerly with Burning Lamp Buddha, did he obtain the dharma? Subhuti answered: No, World-Honored One. When the Tathagata was with Burning Lamp Buddha, he did not obtain the dharma.

[Burning Lamp Buddha] Also translated as Dipankara Buddha, Universal Light Buddha and Fixed Light Buddha. [When the Tathagata was formerly with Burning Lamp Buddha] When the World-Honored One was formerly a bodhisattva of the seventh stage, he met Burning Lamp Buddha and heard the dharma, realized the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas and rose to the eighth stage; Burning Lamp Buddha then gave him the prediction, saying: After ninety-one kalpas from now, in the kalpa named Bhadra, you shall become a Buddha named Shakyamuni. [Prediction] The Buddha’s beforehand recording of a bodhisattva’s name: after how many ages, in such-and-such a place and such-and-such a land, what Buddha he shall become. [Bhadra kalpa] The past great kalpa is called the Adorned kalpa, the future great kalpa is called the Star Constellation kalpa, and the present great kalpa is called the Bhadra kalpa, because in this great kalpa a thousand Buddhas appear in the world, and so it is called the “Bhadra kalpa.”

[When the Tathagata was with Burning Lamp Buddha, he in truth obtained no dharma] Here “he in truth obtained no dharma” has two meanings: from the ultimate standpoint, everything within the dream of ignorance is an illusion, and so he truly obtained no dharma; at the same time, the Tathagata, while in the causal ground, did not cling to having obtained anything—cultivating yet not cultivating, attaining yet not attaining—and so was able to realize the fruit of Buddhahood. In the

Buddha Treasury Sutra, Chapter Eight on Pure Views, the World-Honored One tells in detail of his own cultivation in the causal ground: for a stretch of time and kalpas of immense length, because he clung to having obtained something, the Buddhas did not give him a prediction. For example:

“The Buddha told Shariputra: I recall that in a past life, seeking supreme, perfect enlightenment, I met three billion Buddhas, all named Shakyamuni; at that time I was a wheel-turning sage king and made offerings to them throughout my life, and also to their disciples with clothing, food, bedding and medicine, seeking supreme, perfect enlightenment; yet those Buddhas did not predict of me, ‘In a future age you shall become a Buddha.’ Why is this? Because I had something obtained. Shariputra, I recall that in a past life, in the seventh hundred asamkhyeya kalpa, I met a thousand Buddhas, all named Jambunada; throughout my life I made the four kinds of offerings to them, and they likewise did not give me a prediction, because I had something obtained. Shariputra, I recall that in a past life, also in the seventh hundred asamkhyeya kalpa, I met six million two hundred thousand Buddhas, all named Seeing All Meanings; at that time I was a wheel-turning sage king and made offerings throughout my life of every kind of delightful implement, and also to their disciples, and they likewise did not give me a prediction, because I had something obtained.”
[Causal ground] From the state of an ordinary being first setting the mind on learning Buddhism until the perfection of Buddhahood—this entire process is called the “causal ground.”
This shows that the dharma the Tathagata obtained is illusory and must not be clung to, breaking the mark of dharma.

In the preceding section, Subhuti answered correctly: the four fruits (the fruit of srotapanna, the fruit of sakridagamin, the fruit of anagamin and the fruit of arhat) are all such that in truth no dharma is obtained. Now the World-Honored One again takes his own cultivation in the causal ground as an example, further clarifying the wondrous principle that “in truth no dharma is obtained”: not only are the four fruits of the shravaka in truth unobtained, but even the fruit of Buddhahood that I realized is in truth unobtained. The reason for his counter-question is to bring Subhuti to a silent and heartfelt understanding, and thereby help living beings cut off delusion layer by layer.
In the Great Prajnaparamita Sutra,
fascicle five hundred seventy-one,
the sixth section,
Chapter Nine on Non-Attainment, there is a detailed exposition of “non-attainment”:
“At that time, in the assembly there was a bodhisattva-mahasattva named Good Thought, who asked Supreme
(Supreme Heaven King)

saying: ‘Has the Buddha given the Heaven King the bodhi prediction?’ Supreme answered: ‘Though I have received the prediction, I am still as one dreaming.’ Then Good Thought again asked Supreme: ‘The Heaven King has received the prediction—what has he obtained?’ Supreme answered: ‘Though I have received the prediction, I have obtained nothing.’ Good Thought again said: ‘If one has obtained nothing, what dharma has he not obtained?’ Supreme replied: ‘To have obtained nothing means: not obtaining a self, not obtaining a sentient being, and so on up to not obtaining a knower or a seer, not obtaining the aggregates
(the five aggregates: form, feeling, perception, formation and consciousness)
and the realms
(the eighteen realms; the six sense-faculties, the six dusts and the six consciousnesses together are called the eighteen realms),
the bases

(the twelve bases: the six sense-faculties plus the six dusts together are called the twelve bases. “Bases” means “places of arising”: from the six sense-faculties meeting the six dusts, the six consciousnesses arise),

whether good or not good, whether defiled or pure, whether with outflows or without outflows, whether worldly or world-transcending, whether conditioned or unconditioned, whether birth-and-death or nirvana—of all such things he has obtained nothing.’”
The Heart Sutra says:

“Therefore, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, perception, formation or consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body or mind; no forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; no realm of eye, and so on up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance, and no extinction of ignorance, and so on up to no aging and death, and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, accumulation, extinction or path; no wisdom, and no attainment. Because there is nothing to be attained, the bodhisattva, relying on the prajnaparamita, has no obstruction in his mind. Having no obstruction, he has no fear; far removed from inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate nirvana.”
This says that the five aggregates, the eighteen realms, the twelve links of dependent origination, the four noble truths and the six paramitas are all unobtainable. (See
“A Detailed Explanation of the Heart Sutra”
[Subhuti, what do you think? Has a bodhisattva adorned the Buddha-land? No, World-Honored One. Why is this? What is called adorning the Buddha-land is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning.]

The Buddha asked Subhuti: Subhuti, what do you think—has a bodhisattva, cultivating the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices, adorned the Buddha-land? Subhuti answered: There is no adorning of the Buddha-land, World-Honored One. Why is there none? Because adorning the Buddha-land is a matter within the dream of ignorance, having marks but no essence; it is an illusion.

[Adorning the Buddha-land] To adorn is to deck out and embellish. When a bodhisattva in the causal ground cultivates the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices and dedicates this merit to adorning the dependent-retribution land in which he will dwell when he becomes a Buddha, this is called “adorning the Buddha-land.” [The two retributions] The dependent retribution and the direct retribution. The dependent retribution is the retribution upon which living beings rely for their dwelling, such as lands, the earth, houses and implements; the direct retribution is the body falsely compounded of the five aggregates, which living beings are moved to receive through delusion and karma.

In the sentence “what is called adorning the Buddha-land is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning,” “what is called adorning the Buddha-land” means that in terms of marks, there is such a thing as adorning the Buddha-land. “Is not adorning” means that in terms of reality there is no such thing as adorning the Buddha-land, because adorning the Buddha-land is a matter within the dream of ignorance and does not truly exist; this is called having no essence (having no true substance). “Therefore it is called adorning” means: this illusion, which has marks but no essence, is what people call adorning the Buddha-land.

In the fifth section, the Buddha says: “All forms whatsoever are false and unreal.” Therefore the sutra repeatedly uses the formula “having marks, without essence, is illusion” to judge illusions. For example: “What is called adorning the Buddha-land (having marks) is not adorning (without essence); therefore it is called adorning (it is illusion).” This is the famous three-part formula: “is (having marks), is not (without essence), therefore is called (what has marks but no essence is illusion).”

What is called adorning the Buddha-land is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning”—here too there are two meanings: from the ultimate standpoint, everything within the dream of ignorance is an illusion, and so it is truly “not adorning.” At the same time, if a bodhisattva does not cling to this, then what he cultivates is merit and virtue, and he can adorn the Buddha-land; if a bodhisattva clings to this, then what he cultivates is outflows-tainted merit (outflow is another name for affliction, and “with outflows” means having afflictions), and he cannot adorn the Buddha-land. Therefore it is said: what is called adorning the Buddha-land is not adorning; therefore it is called adorning.
This shows that adorning the Buddha-land is illusory and must not be clung to, breaking the mark of dharma.

[Therefore, Subhuti, all bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.]

One should not dwell in the six dusts and give rise to a mind of discursive thought, but should leave marks and give rise to a pure mind—this is the essential secret of cultivation. Now the World-Honored One teaches: “All bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere (that is, they should give rise to a mind in a place where there is nothing to dwell upon).”
[They should give rise to a mind in a place where there is nothing to dwell upon] This means that whatever thoughts arise, none of them cling to marks.
Therefore, Subhuti, all bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind”
—Therefore, Subhuti, all great bodhisattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind.

Therefore” is a summarizing word linking what precedes and what follows. The World-Honored One tells Subhuti: as has been said above, the dharma that the Tathagata obtained is illusion, and the bodhisattva’s cultivation in adorning the Buddha-land is likewise illusion. Therefore, understanding that all marks are illusion, that in truth nothing is done and nothing is obtained, all bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to a pure mind: “they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” We living beings, since beginningless kalpas, have transmigrated through the six paths and endured every torment, precisely because we cling to marks and give rise to mind—and what we cling to is illusion. Truly this is an injustice as vast as heaven! Therefore the Diamond Sutra lays bare the truth and dissolves my inverted thoughts of a billion kalpas.

[Bodhisattva-mahasattva] That is, a great bodhisattva. Here “all bodhisattvas-mahasattvas,” as in the third section, refers to the good men and good women who have set their minds on supreme, perfect enlightenment; this designation expresses the World-Honored One’s boundless expectations of them. [Should thus give rise to a pure mind] All the things listed above are illusions, and so bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should no longer be turned by circumstances or by dharmas; in the face of circumstances and dharmas they should be their own masters, “no longer having the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan; no mark of dharma, and no mark of non-dharma.”

Since the Tathagata cannot obtain any dharma, and a bodhisattva cannot adorn the Buddha-land either, and all is illusion, what desire or obstruction remains? Therefore the great bodhisattvas should cultivate a pure mind according to “they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”—not deluded by marks, not turned by circumstances; only thus can one awaken from the great dream. Cultivation is precisely the cultivation of a pure mind. The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“To leave marks outwardly is Chan; not to be disturbed inwardly is samadhi. Outer Chan and inner samadhi—this is called meditative concentration.”
They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”

—One should not cling to the dust-objects (the dust of forms, the dust of sounds, the dust of smells, the dust of tastes, the dust of tangibles and the dust of dharmas) and give rise to a mind of discursive thought (a mind of discrimination, calculation, love and hate, grasping and rejecting); one should give rise to a pure mind that dwells nowhere (one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere and is unstained by the dust-objects).

Here “dwell” means to cling to marks and give rise to a discriminating mind—falsely grasping at circumstances and marks as real, and so loving, hating, grasping and rejecting. “Give rise to mind” means to give rise to thoughts. To give rise to mind while clinging to marks is delusion; to give rise to mind without clinging to marks is wisdom. Here “grasping” means seeking, and “rejecting” means avoiding. The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra says:

“The mind of a bodhisattva is always empty and quiescent, without any false thoughts, neither arising nor ceasing, neither moving nor shaking—this is the pure mind. The mind of an ordinary being arises and ceases with ignorance, is inverted in false thoughts, grasps and rejects good and evil, and holds views of ordinary being and sage—this is called the turbid and disordered mind. ‘They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms’: if the mind is pure, it is not confused and disordered by any circumstance.”
They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”

Here there are two levels. “They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas” means not giving rise to thoughts toward circumstances; “they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere” means giving rise to thoughts yet dwelling nowhere (not taking forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles and dharmas as real).

Not giving rise to a mind dwelling in forms, sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles and dharmas—this is the state of Chan Master Wolun in the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch, “toward circumstances the mind does not arise.” This too is a state of a certain height, but it has samadhi without wisdom, and so is not yet ultimate. Giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere is the Sixth Patriarch’s state of “toward circumstances the mind arises again and again,” the equal holding of samadhi and wisdom; and it is what the Vimalakirti Sutra,
Chapter One on the Buddha-Land, says:
“One can skillfully distinguish the marks of all dharmas, yet in the supreme truth one does not move.”
(One can clearly discern all dharmas, yet the mind is not moved by these illusions.) And it is also what the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Though the six sense-faculties
(eye, ear, nose, tongue, body and mind)
have seeing, hearing, sensing and knowing, they are not stained by the ten thousand circumstances, and the true nature is ever at ease.”
[The supreme truth] The highest and most supreme principle, namely the true nature of all dharmas. The Buddha says:

“All dharmas are false; wherever they cease, that is called the real, is called the true nature, is called the dharma-realm, is named ultimate wisdom, is named the supreme truth, is named the supreme truth of emptiness.”
(Mahaparinirvana Sutra,
fascicle forty,
Chapter on Kaundinya.)
[They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere]

“Dwell” means to dwell and cling—to take circumstances and conditions as real (clinging to marks). “Dwell nowhere” means not to take any circumstance or condition as real (leaving marks). “They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere” means: one should give rise to mind without taking any circumstance or condition as real (leaving marks); this is also what the later passage, “Leaving Marks and Quiescence, Section Fourteen,” calls “one should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.” This mind that dwells nowhere is the pure mind of a bodhisattva who, within the dream, knows it to be a dream. (This sutra says:
“All bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should thus give rise to
a pure mind
: they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.”
) Master Taixu says:
“The mind within the dream is the mind of an ordinary being;
the mind that knows the dream within the dream is the mind of a bodhisattva
; the mind awakened from the dream is the mind of a Buddha.”
(Outline of Consciousness-Only Contemplation) Therefore this sutra says:

“If a bodhisattva has the mark of self, the mark of a person, the mark of sentient beings or the mark of a lifespan, he is not a bodhisattva.” “If a bodhisattva gives in giving without dwelling in marks
(giving while dwelling nowhere)
, his merit and virtue is inconceivable.” “A bodhisattva, toward dharmas, should
dwell nowhere
and practice giving.” “Good men and good women who set their minds on supreme, perfect enlightenment
should give rise to such a mind

: I should bring all living beings to extinction and deliverance, and after bringing all living beings to extinction and deliverance, not one living being has in truth been brought to extinction and deliverance
(dwelling nowhere while saving living beings)
The Great Prajnaparamita Sutra,
fascicle one,
Chapter on Learning the Contemplations, says:
“All bodhisattvas-mahasattvas should take
non-attachment
(dwelling nowhere)
as skillful means and perfect the prajnaparamita, because the nature and marks of all dharmas are unobtainable.”
“Non-attachment” means not clinging to marks, which is leaving marks.
Daoxin, the Fourth Patriarch of Chan, says:

“In circumstances there is no fair or foul; the fair and foul arise within the mind. If the mind will not force names on things, whence could deluded feelings ever rise? And when deluded feelings no longer rise, the true mind knows all things, at liberty.”
Here “if the mind does not force names upon them” is precisely giving rise to a pure mind that dwells nowhere.
Maitreya Bodhisattva says:

“Discrimination is consciousness; non-discrimination is wisdom. Relying on consciousness, one is defiled; relying on wisdom, one is pure. In defilement there is birth and death; in purity there are no Buddhas.”
(Dream Roam Collection,
“The Autobiographical Chronological Record of Old Man Hanshan”)
The Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch,
Chapter Four on Concentration and Wisdom, says:
“The deluded person has thoughts toward circumstances, and on those thoughts then gives rise to wrong views; all the dust-toil and false thoughts arise from this.”

Therefore one should not cling to circumstances and give rise to mind, that is, “they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas.”

They should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas”—for those who recite the Buddha’s name this is of the utmost importance. The layman Jiang Weinong says in his Commentary on the Diamond Sutra:

“That one should not dwell means that the student should be aware and illumined upon consciousness, and not give rise to clinging and discrimination.” “In the work of Buddha-recitation, though one may not yet be able to recite without reciting, if only one’s practice and vows are genuine and earnest, then by relying on the power of Amitabha’s compassionate vows one will also be received and guided to rebirth, and will be equal to an avaivartika—which is to say, non-retrogression—that is, the stage of initial dwelling. To reach this stage by cultivating other methods, one must pass through long, distant kalpas; now it is brought about in a single lifetime—how much more could be said of its being the most expedient of expedients! … Yet for practice and vows to be genuine and earnest, one’s whole mind must be fixed on reciting the Buddha’s name and seeking rebirth; only then can it be called genuine and earnest. If one recites the Buddha’s name on the one hand and on the other gives rise to thoughts of dust and turbidity, then one’s practice and vows are not genuine and earnest. Therefore, as for the matter of cutting off thoughts, even if a reciter of the Buddha’s name finds it hard to accomplish, the two lines ‘they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas’ must certainly be carried out. Otherwise, if the vows are not earnest and the practice is not genuine, how can one be received and guided by the Buddha? Why is this? When the breath of dust and turbidity is heavy, it accords all too little with the two words ‘pure and clean,’ and then even the Buddha can do nothing about it!”
[Reciting without reciting] To recite the Buddha’s name with no-thought (not giving rise to a single thought)—this is reciting the Buddha of true nature, reciting the dharmakaya Buddha. (See
“Reciting Without Reciting”
Give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”—to know all dharmas as illusion and not be dragged, bound or turned by them, which is what the Platform Sutra of the Sixth Patriarch says:
“Cause the six consciousnesses to go out through the six gates, and within the six dusts be neither stained nor mixed; come and go freely, functioning without obstruction.”
The Record of the Mirror of the Source says:

“Chan Master Anguo says: The sutra says, ‘They should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere.’ Dwelling nowhere means not dwelling in forms, not dwelling in sounds, not dwelling in delusion, not dwelling in awakening, not dwelling in essence, not dwelling in function. ‘Giving rise to mind’ means that in every place the one mind is manifested. If one dwells in good and gives rise to mind, good appears; if one dwells in evil and gives rise to mind, evil appears; and the original mind is then hidden. If one dwells nowhere, the ten directions and worlds are only the one mind. Truly know that ‘it is not the wind and banner that move, but the mind that moves.’”
The Great Compendium of a Hundred Commentaries on the Diamond Sutra says:

“The mind of living beings is fundamentally without dwelling, but because circumstances come and touch it, it then gives rise to mind. Not knowing that the touched circumstance is empty, one supposes worldly dharmas to be real and so dwells the mind upon circumstances. It is just like a monkey grasping at the moon
(the moon in the water)
or a diseased eye seeing flowers
(empty flowers)

—all the ten thousand dharmas arise from the mind. If one awakens to the true nature, then one dwells nowhere. The mind that dwells nowhere is wisdom, without any affliction, like great emptiness, without obstruction. The mind that dwells somewhere is false thought; the six dusts contend and arise, like floating clouds coming and going without fixedness.”
Question: If one does not give rise to mind, how is one to live and work?

Answer: “Not giving rise to mind” means not giving rise to mind while clinging to marks; that is, giving rise to mind without clinging to marks (not taking circumstances and conditions as real). When things come, do them; when things go, be quiescent. When doing things, do not cling to marks (do not take circumstances as real; within the dream, know it to be a dream); act in accordance with principle, with single-minded devotion, without entertaining false thoughts.

[Subhuti, suppose there were a person whose body were like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains; what do you think—would that body be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One. Why is this? The Buddha says it is not a body; therefore it is called a great body.]

The Buddha asked: Subhuti, suppose there were a person whose body were like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains; what do you think—would this body be great? Subhuti answered: Very great, World-Honored One. Why is this body said to be very great? Because this body is an illusion (the Buddha says it is not a body), and so there can be talk of great and small (great and small being concepts within the dream of ignorance).

[Mount Sumeru, king of mountains] That is, Mount Sumeru; because it is the highest and greatest, and is made of the four treasures—gold, silver, lapis lazuli and crystal—no other mountain can compare with it, and it is the king of mountains; hence it is called Mount Sumeru, king of mountains. “Mount Sumeru” is rendered into Chinese as Wonderful High Mountain, and is the center of a small world. [A body like Mount Sumeru, king of mountains] A body as tall, great, wondrous and fair as Mount Sumeru. The “body” here is the supreme wondrous reward-body, the body of boundless marks and excellences that a bodhisattva can realize only after diligently cultivating the six paramitas and the ten thousand practices through many kalpas, with merit and wisdom complete. This body is subtle and wondrous; though it has form and marks, none but a bodhisattva on the groundings can see it. (From the bodhisattva of initial dwelling up to the Buddha, all have three bodies: the dharma-body, the reward-body and the response-body.)

Just now the World-Honored One taught the rule of the pure mind (“they should not give rise to a mind dwelling in forms, nor give rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; they should give rise to a mind that dwells nowhere”). Now he brings up this topic of the supreme wondrous reward-body, which cultivators find most interesting, to see how well Subhuti has grasped and mastered this rule of the pure mind. Subhuti’s first words in reply, “very great,” are like a mirror reflecting an object—this is correct. In the second sentence he says that this body is an illusion, guarding the original mind tightly and not being dragged by circumstances. This shows that the Venerable Subhuti has not only grasped the rule of the pure mind but applies it very well, setting us an example: every thought abides in the Way.

The Blue Cliff Record recounts: Mazu and his disciple Baizhang were walking together when they saw a wild duck fly past. The Patriarch said: What is that? Baizhang said: A wild duck. The Patriarch said: Where has it gone? (testing whether Baizhang gave rise to a mind dwelling in forms) Baizhang said: It has flown away. The Patriarch then twisted Baizhang’s nose, and Baizhang cried out in pain. The Patriarch said: When did it ever fly away! At these words Baizhang had an awakening.

Baizhang’s first reply, “a wild duck,” was like a mirror reflecting a thing—that was correct. But his second reply, “it has flown away,” was giving rise to a mind dwelling in forms, chasing things along with circumstances, failing to guard the original mind (losing right mindfulness). Therefore Mazu twisted his nose, to make him turn back and guard the original mind. In the midst of the pain Baizhang heard his teacher say: When did it ever fly away? (The wild duck is an illusion—how could there be coming or going?) and he suddenly awakened: “one should thus give rise to a pure mind.” (Mazu twisted Baizhang’s nose precisely to make him never forget to guard the original mind at all times, and never chase things along with circumstances.)
[When did it ever fly away] Gathering marks back into the nature, and emptying them into emptiness.
All forms whatsoever are false and unreal.”

If one does not leave marks, it is hard to awaken to the Way; therefore Mazu used the thunderbolt method of a lightning flash that leaves no time to stop the ears, striking at Baizhang’s unawakened mind. The Vajrasamadhi Sutra says:
“‘If one loses the original mind, one should at once repent’—this dharma is coolness and refreshment.”
From this one may glimpse the conduct of a strict teacher and a worthy disciple, and it lets us intimately feel that “the fragrance of plum blossoms comes from the bitter cold.”

Above we spoke of the unconditioned dharma (not giving rise to a mind dwelling in forms, not giving rise to a mind dwelling in sounds, smells, tastes, tangibles or dharmas; giving rise to a mind that dwells nowhere); this section speaks of receiving and upholding this sutra and cultivating while leaving marks—the unconditioned dharma—whose merit and virtue is supremely excellent.

[Subhuti, if there were as many Ganges Rivers as the grains of sand in the Ganges, what do you think—would the sand of all those Ganges Rivers be many? Subhuti said: Very many, World-Honored One. Why, even those Ganges Rivers alone are countless in number, how much more their sand.]

The World-Honored One asked: Subhuti, if the sand in the Ganges were taken—one grain of sand for each Ganges River—what do you think, would the sand of all those Ganges Rivers be many? (Mathematically speaking, suppose the number of grains of sand in one Ganges River is

) are already countless in number, how much more the sand of those Ganges Rivers (

Master Kumarajiva’s translation is superb! Not only is the language concise and apt, but it rises and falls with cadence, pleasant to read aloud.

[Subhuti, I now tell you in truth. If good men and good women were to fill with seven treasures as many trichiliocosms as the sand of all those Ganges Rivers, and give them away in giving, would the merit obtained be great? Subhuti said: Very great, World-Honored One.]
Subhuti, I now tell you in truth. If good men and good women were to take as many seven treasures as would fill all the trichiliocosms of the number of all the sand in those Ganges Rivers of yours (
N
times
N
), and give them away in giving, would the merit obtained be great? Subhuti answered: Very great, World-Honored One.

[I now tell you in truth] After the word “you” in “I now tell you in truth” there should be a period, and its meaning runs through to the end of this section, “and this merit and virtue surpasses the former merit and virtue.”

[The Buddha told Subhuti: If good men and good women receive and uphold even four lines of verse from this sutra and explain them for others, this merit and virtue surpasses the former merit and virtue.]

The Buddha told Subhuti: If there are good men and good women who, from this sutra, receive and uphold even four lines of verse and explain them for others, this merit and virtue surpasses the former merit and virtue.

This says that however many the seven treasures, it is still giving with marks; whereas receiving and upholding this sutra and explaining it for others is giving without marks, and so its merit and virtue is all the greater.
The World-Honored One further teaches the supreme excellence of this sutra. “True teaching” refers to the Buddha’s teaching in this sutra.

[Furthermore, Subhuti, wherever this sutra is spoken, even four lines of verse, you should know that that place is one which all the gods, humans and asuras of every world should worship and make offerings to, as to a Buddha’s stupa and temple. How much more so if there is a person who can receive, uphold and recite the whole of it.]

Not only that (continuing from the above), Subhuti: whenever, wherever and for whatever reason this Diamond Sutra is spoken—whether in whole, in part, or even as few as four lines—you should know that the place where it is spoken is most honored and rare, and that all the gods, humans and asuras of every world (the three good paths) should come there to protect the dharma and make offerings, as to a Buddha’s stupa and temple. If simply speaking four lines of verse brings merit such as this, how much more so if there is a person who can faithfully accept, uphold, recite and read the whole of it.

[Wherever it is spoken] Whenever, wherever and for whatever reason it is spoken. [Gods, humans and asuras] Gods, humans and asuras—these are the three good paths of the world. [Asura] One of the six paths, rendered into Chinese as “non-god,” because they have the blessings of gods but not the virtue of gods, resembling gods yet not being gods.
[Subhuti, you should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost and rarest dharma. Wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, and there are revered disciples.]

Subhuti, you should know that such a person will accomplish the most supreme, foremost and rarest dharma of supreme, perfect enlightenment. Wherever the Diamond Sutra is, it is as though the Buddha were here, and it should be revered as disciples revere the Buddha.
[And revered disciples] “Revered as disciples” means revered just as disciples revere the Buddha. The Yuan Wei

dynasty translation by Bodhiruci reads: “Subhuti! You should know that such a person accomplishes the most supreme, foremost and rarest dharma. Wherever this sutra is, there is the Buddha, revered as like the Buddha.”

The above shows that receiving and upholding, reciting and reading the Diamond Sutra, expounding the Diamond Sutra, and the place where the Diamond Sutra is—all are honored and rare beyond compare, making one understand the surpassing excellence of this Dharma-gate of leaving illusion and becoming a Buddha.
